title: Data Destruction and Sanitization
objective: Study-guide review — CISSP — Domain 2: Asset Security: Data Destruction and Sanitization.

items: Clearing — Overwriting data with zeros/patterns; protects against casual recovery
Purging — More intensive removal; protects against lab-based attacks (degaussing, crypto-erase)
Destruction — Physical destruction of media (shredding, incineration, disintegration)
Method selection depends on data classification and media type
NIST SP 800-88 provides guidelines for media sanitization

blocks.text: From Chapple: "Erasing a file doesn't delete it. Clearing media overwrites it with zeros or patterns. Purging uses more intensive methods. Destruction physically destroys the media." Degaussing: Uses a powerful magnetic field to erase magnetic media (hard drives, tapes). NOT effective on solid-state drives (SSDs) or optical media because they don't use magnetic storage. ⚠️ Exam Trap: Degaussing does NOT work on SSDs! SSDs require different sanitization methods (crypto-erase, physical destruction, or manufacturer secure erase commands). The exam tests this distinction.

items: Data remanence — Residual data remaining after deletion or sanitization attempts
Simple deletion only removes the file pointer, not the actual data
Formatting may not completely remove all data
Overwriting multiple times reduces but may not eliminate remanence
Physical destruction is the only guaranteed method to eliminate all remanence

blocks.text: Data remanence is the biggest concern when decommissioning or repurposing storage media. Even after deletion, data may remain:

items: File deletion — Only removes directory entry; data blocks remain intact
Quick format — Rebuilds file system structure; data blocks remain
Full format — May overwrite data blocks once; may not eliminate all remanence
Single overwrite — Generally sufficient for most purposes (NIST SP 800-88 guidance)
Multiple overwrites — Provides additional assurance but diminishing returns

blocks.text: For highly classified data, physical destruction is the only acceptable method.

items: Encrypts data first, then destroys the encryption key
Data becomes unrecoverable without the key
Effective for cloud environments where physical destruction isn't possible
Faster than traditional overwriting methods
Requires strong encryption to be effective

blocks.text: Cryptographic erasure (crypto-erase) is increasingly important in cloud environments where you don't have physical access to storage media. The process:

items: Encrypt all data with a strong key (e.g., AES-256)
When data must be destroyed, securely destroy the encryption key
Without the key, the encrypted data is computationally infeasible to recover

blocks.text: This approach is approved by NIST SP 800-88 as a valid purging method. It is particularly useful for:

items: Cloud storage services
Solid-state drives (SSDs) where degaussing doesn't work
Self-encrypting drives (SEDs) with hardware encryption

blocks.title: Exam trap
blocks.text: ⚠️ Exam Trap: Crypto-erase only works if the original encryption was strong. Weak encryption = weak erasure. Also, if key copies exist anywhere (backup, escrow), the data is not truly destroyed.
